original_value: Digital heritage comprises a broad variety of approaches and topics and involves researchers from multiple disciplines. Against this background, this article presents a four-stage investigation on standards, publications, disciplinary cultures, as well as scholars in the field of digital heritage and particularly tangible objects as monuments and sites, carried out in 2016 and 2017. It includes results of (1) the inquiry of nearly 4,000 publications from major conferences, (2) a workshop-based survey involving 44 researchers, (3) 15 qualitative interviews, as well as (4) two online surveys with 1,000 and 700 participants, respectively. As an overall finding, the community is driven by researchers from European countries, especially Italy, with a background in humanities. Cross-national co-authorships are promoted by cultural and spatial closeness and—probably due to funding policy—EU membership. A discourse is primarily driven by technologies, and the most common keywords refer to the technologies used. Most prominent research areas are data acquisition and management, visualization, and analysis. Recent topics are, for instance, unmanned airborne vehicle (UAV)-based 3D surveying technologies, augmented and virtual reality visualization, metadata and paradata standards for documentation, and virtual museums. Since a lack of money is named as the biggest obstacle nowadays, competency and human resources are most frequently named as demand. An epistemic culture in the scholarly field of digital heritage is closer to engineering than to humanities. Moreover, conference series are most relevant for a scientific discourse, and especially EU projects set pace as most important research endeavors.

result.paraphrase: Digital heritage spans a wide range of methods and subjects and brings together researchers from many disciplines. In this context, the article reports a four-part study of standards, publications, disciplinary cultures, and scholars working in digital heritage, with particular attention to tangible objects such as monuments and sites, conducted in 2016 and 2017. It draws on (1) a review of nearly 4,000 publications from major conferences, (2) a workshop survey of 44 researchers, (3) 15 qualitative interviews, and (4) two online surveys with 1,000 and 700 participants, respectively. Overall, the field is led by researchers from European countries, especially Italy, and by scholars with a humanities background. Cross-border coauthorship is encouraged by cultural and geographic proximity and, probably because of funding policy, EU membership. The discourse is shaped mainly by technology, and the most frequent keywords point to the technologies in use. The leading research areas are data acquisition and management, visualization, and analysis. Recent topics include UAV-based 3D surveying technologies, augmented and virtual reality visualization, metadata and paradata standards for documentation, and virtual museums. As funding shortages are identified as the main current obstacle, competence and human resources are most often cited as needs. The field’s epistemic culture is closer to engineering than to the humanities. In addition, conference series are the most important venue for scholarly discourse, and EU projects in particular are regarded as the key drivers of research.
